vignette: Case Vignette: David David, an 18-year-old male of Oceania ethnicity, has been grappling with significant psychological distress stemming from his childhood experience of witnessing domestic violence. Growing up, he often found himself alone in the home when his father would come back intoxicated, creating a toxic environment that left lasting scars. Now working as a Project Manager and in a relationship, David's life is structured around avoiding triggers that remind him of those traumatic moments. Being alone with men or hearing the distinct smell of alcohol instantly brings back vivid fragments of the violence he witnessed. The mere presence of these triggers can send him into a heightened state of anxiety. For instance, when David is on his bicycle and passes by someone drinking outside a bar, his heart rate spikes, and he feels an overwhelming urge to flee. David’s maladaptive strategies have become deeply ingrained as coping mechanisms for dealing with the overwhelming fear that these triggers evoke. He frequently turns to smoking and occasional substance use to numb himself from the terror that arises when confronted with reminders of his traumatic past. When he smells alcohol or sees a man alone in an elevator at work, he finds solace in cigarettes to calm himself down, often feeling as though it is the only thing keeping him grounded. The memories associated with the trauma are fragmented and incomplete. David feels like he can only recall parts of what happened, leaving large gaps that fill him with uncertainty and dread. Recalling these moments brings back intense feelings of terror, which can be so overwhelming that he finds himself isolated and struggling to function normally. His fragmented memories often surface unexpectedly during the day, causing him to abruptly stop whatever he is doing and withdraw into his own thoughts. David’s heightened state of threat perception is closely tied to these memories and triggers. He constantly checks locks on doors and windows multiple times a day, ensuring that there are no vulnerabilities that could lead to another traumatic event. Ordinary sounds that would not bother most people can make him jump or startle, causing him to watch other people for signs of potential harm. This constant vigilance has made it difficult for him to fully engage in his work as a Project Manager, often leading to moments where he is distracted and unable to focus on tasks at hand. His memories also exacerbate his maladaptive behaviors, making them more frequent and intense. When David feels that he cannot piece together what happened or when terror grips him upon recalling the event, he tends to retreat into substance use as a means of escaping these overwhelming feelings. This cycle has led to significant distress in both his professional life and relationship. David’s current state is marked by an acute sense of vulnerability and fear. He is most afraid that another traumatic event will occur, pushing him further into isolation and dependence on maladaptive strategies for coping with the constant threat he feels. It was a particularly frightening incident at work, where he felt cornered in an elevator by a man drinking alcohol, that finally motivated him to seek help. Despite his fears, David is hopeful that therapy can provide tools to manage his distress and regain control over his life. David’s journey toward recovery begins with understanding the complex interplay between his triggers, maladaptive strategies, threat perceptions, and fragmented memories. His case highlights the need for a comprehensive approach that addresses these interconnected elements, ultimately helping him navigate his daily experiences without being overwhelmed by the past.
